summary: Sirach 40 begins with a sober description of human life under anxiety, labor, mortality, and night fears, from rulers to the lowly. It then contrasts the passing goods of injustice with kindness, almsgiving, counsel, and the fear of the Lord. The chapter ends with a warning against dependence on another person’s table and the humiliation of begging.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach’s wisdom teaching facing mortality and social vulnerability directly. It places ordinary goods in a ranked order, repeatedly asking what lasts when wealth, status, and comfort do not.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson’s translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC and was likely complete around 180–175 BC. The grandson arrived in Egypt around 132 BC and translated it during his stay.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, ordinary social life, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean pressures in view.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction in poetic sayings, comparisons, catalogues, and ranked maxims.

outline.heading: Human Life Under a Heavy Yoke
outline.note: The chapter opens by describing travail, fear of death, restless nights, and terrifying dreams as common human burdens.

outline.heading: Death and Calamity
outline.note: The scope widens to all creatures, then especially sinners, naming death, violence, famine, suffering, plague, and the return of earthly and watery things to their places.

outline.heading: What Fails and What Stands
outline.note: Bribery, injustice, unjust goods, and ungodly descendants are pictured as temporary, while good faith, kindness, and almsgiving endure.

outline.heading: Better Than Both
outline.note: A chain of comparisons ranks contentment, treasure, family, wisdom, speech, friendship, counsel, and especially the fear of the Lord.

outline.heading: The Shame of Begging
outline.note: The final sayings warn the son against a beggar’s life, dependence on another person’s table, and shameless begging.

keyVerses.text: Great travail is created for every man. A heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day of their coming forth from their mother’s womb, until the day for their burial in the mother of all things.
keyVerses.why: This first verse states the chapter’s broad claim: ordinary human life is weighed down from birth to burial.

keyVerses.text: All bribery and injustice will be blotted out. Good faith will stand forever.
keyVerses.why: This sentence turns the chapter from human misery toward moral contrast, distinguishing what disappears from what endures.

keyVerses.text: Kindness is like a garden of blessings. Almsgiving endures forever.
keyVerses.why: The verse names two practices that Sirach presents as lasting goods in contrast to unjust wealth.

keyVerses.text: Riches and strength will lift up the heart. The fear of the Lord is better than both. There is nothing lacking in the fear of the Lord. In it, there is no need to seek help.
keyVerses.why: This is the peak of the chapter’s repeated “better than both” pattern, placing reverence for the Lord above wealth and power.

themes: human anxiety from birth to burial
the temporary nature of unjust gain
the fear of the Lord as security

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin so darkly?
questions.answer: The opening verses describe human life as marked by travail, fear, and restlessness. Sirach does not begin with an exception for the powerful: the burden reaches from the one on a throne to the one in earth and ashes. The point is not that every life feels identical, but that mortality and anxiety belong to the whole human condition.

questions.question: What is the “heavy yoke” in verse 1?
questions.answer: In this chapter, the “heavy yoke” is the burden of life under travail, expectation, death, fear, conflict, and unrest. The following verses define it by description rather than by a technical term. It is not limited to poverty or political oppression, because the text applies it from throne to burlap.

questions.question: Why does Sirach spend so much space on sleep and dreams?
questions.answer: Verses 5-7 picture a person who cannot even find peace in bed. Sleep becomes like keeping watch, and the dreamer feels as if he has escaped battle before waking and realizing the fear was nothing. The image makes anxiety bodily and ordinary, not merely theoretical.

questions.question: Does verse 10 say God created disasters for wicked people?
questions.answer: Verse 10 says, “All these things were created for the wicked,” after listing death, bloodshed, strife, sword, calamities, famine, suffering, and plague. Yet verse 8 has already said troubles reach all living creatures, with sinners suffering sevenfold. The passage intensifies its account of universal hardship into judgment language; it does not explain every instance of suffering or make suffering itself proof of wickedness.

questions.question: What does the flood have to do with this chapter?
questions.answer: The flood is mentioned only briefly in verse 10, connected with wickedness and the calamities just listed. The chapter does not retell the flood story or develop its details. Here it functions as an example of judgment associated with human wickedness.

questions.question: What contrast is made between injustice and good faith?
questions.answer: Verses 12-16 describe bribery, injustice, unjust goods, lawbreakers, and ungodly descendants as things that fail, dry up, or are uprooted. In contrast, verse 12 says good faith will stand forever, and verse 17 says kindness and almsgiving endure. The chapter’s moral contrast is between gain that cannot last and faithful conduct that does.

questions.question: Why does the chapter keep saying one thing is better than two others?
questions.answer: Verses 18-27 use repeated comparisons to train judgment. Work with contentment, treasure, children, a city, wine, music, beauty, friendship, money, strength, counsel, and the fear of the Lord are placed in relation to one another. The pattern does not deny that ordinary goods are good; it ranks them.

questions.question: What does “the fear of the Lord” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, fear of the Lord is better than riches and strength, has “nothing lacking,” and is like “a garden of blessing.” Across Sirach it means practiced allegiance and reverence, not merely panic. Here it names a more secure good than wealth, power, or glory.

questions.question: Is the warning against begging a command to despise poor people?
questions.answer: The final verses warn the addressed “son” against a beggar’s dependence on another person’s table. Their claim that death is preferable to begging is a harsh expression of ancient shame about dependence, not a measure of a poor person’s worth. The same chapter praises almsgiving in verses 17 and 24, so its warning does not cancel the duty to help people in need.

glossary.def: Hard labor, distress, or painful toil; the chapter uses it for the burden created for every person.
A weight or burden placed on someone; here it describes the pressure of human life from birth to burial.
Coarse cloth associated here with low status, contrasted with purple and a crown.
Giving help to the needy; this chapter says it endures forever and rescues better than relatives and helpers.
Reverent allegiance to the Lord; in this chapter it is valued above riches, strength, and glory.
